Title: MY SIDE of the Succubus story...What happened in LA!

Messages.Author: Mike Courtois
Messages.Body:
Let me first state that ANY use of the word "Collusion" regarding the
afore mentioned tournament round is a COMPLETE TRAVISTY AND UTTERLY
BEWILDERING!!!!! This word "Collusion" is thrown around, often
flipantly, by bitter and badly beaten Methusalas on the wrong side of
a devestating deal. Lets get one one thing perfectly straight, I WAS
DEAD IN THAT ROUND! By Brad (my pred), or Paul (my NEW pred through
Kindred Restucture) both had VERY good stops to my deck and neither
even knew it. To be sure, I KNEW I was dead.

To make a long story short, I don't care what ANYBODY says, Brad made
a deal with Paul without FULLY outlining the terms of the deal. As
anyone who's ever played with our group knows, it was a GREVIOUS
ERROR! Paul played Brad like a $2 Fiddle! I saw it coming THE WHOLE
TIME! Brad to his unsettled dismay did not! He then wanted to go back
in the turn sequence and re-block the vote that he had already
declined to block. Only after a Judge's Final ruling did he
reluctantly conceed to the failed, out of sequence block. Not to
mention the Wake that he clearly played, of his own free will, yet it
was the Judge again forcing him to declare the card played, after
decietfully insisting to the judge the card "fell out of my hand". I
was truly disappointed by this display of player sportsmanship here.
He was just bitter at being suckered and he had no one to blame except
himself.

At any rate Paul's dupe had suceeded and the Methuselas switched
places. It was Paul's intention to kill me and continue with the game,
scribing the most victory points he could take. But the argument
between Paul and Brad continued. Not only did it continue but it
escallated with unsportsmanlike comments flying from both sides, while
the rest of the table just waited and I myself waited for my eventual
death from Paul. The argument between Brad and Paul crescendoed with
Paul's realization that the only way for Paul to secure any victory
points from a table that had just ganged up on him, was to create an
unholy alliance with the controller of the Succubus Club. Me.

Before I showed up to this convention, I had purchased my tickets for
Gencon and it was my intention to qualify, using any legal means
available to me via the tournament rules of VTES. I got what I came
for. By the skin of my teeth, using all the legal resources afforded
by my deck, out of 41 players, in what I would gather was the largest
single tournament ever attended by anyone in the Western US, I managed
to qualify 10th. I am proud of my play!

Do I like the Succubus Club? No. Do I think it should be banned from
tournaments? Yes. Why then, you may ask, did I play with the Succubus
Club? Because it helped me achieve my victory points. Brad stated that
he would put Succubus Clubs in every one of his decks in hopes of
proving the card broken. I wish him success. I also will continue to
prove that this card should be banned from tournament play. In the
meantime, Arson is a fairly good card. I currently don't like Weenie
Decks either, but I also accept that it's part of the game and I am
responsable for making adjustments as needed.

I'll conclude with this: The thing I love most about VTES are the
friends that I meet along the way. I just met a wonderful player from
France.(Hi, Renya!)He is now a friend. That's worth 1,000 Victory
Points. We have to remember what we are doing here. It's just a game.
A fairly intense game at times, but nonetheless, just a game. I hope
to see all of you continuing to come to our conventions in LA. It
really is a lot of fun.

Thanks for your time,
Mike

Yes and no. It was rather unfortunate and completely unnecessary for Mike to
make any comments about what transpired in that particular game which caused
Mike and Paul to ally. I don't believe Brad did so I don't understand the need
to tell anyone's "side of the story" other than what side of the Succubus Club
they happened to be sitting on when the alliance happened. But Mike's Succubus
Club had an undeniable influence on the game.

The _point_ is that once the tightly-woven alliance came into being, it was
the Succubus Club that went a long ways towards making it an unstoppable alliance.
I was Mike's first prey after the Restructure (and before for that matter) and
while I got stuck very badly due to the restructure happening at all - which was
a legitimate tactic IMO - Mike having some of Paul's minions at essentially no cost

it hopeless even had I not been screwed out of all my bleed work up to the point of
the restructure. So say what you want about alliances for victory point being OK
or bad, the fact is that they're _much_ easier to work with the Succubus Club. So
much so that, IMHO - and apparently in Mike's opinion as well - that it detracts
from the game the way any unbalanced card or tactic that's too easy win with detracts
from a strategy game.

I don't understand this yet. Paul had just done a Kindred Restructure
to make you his prey and, from what you say, was almost certain to get
a VP and 6 pool by ousting you. Instead of doing this, the deal was
that he give all his stuff to you, you get 3 VP and then he would
depend upon your good will to gain 2 VP at the end.

If one assumes that there was no collusion designed mainly to help you
win, this only makes sense if he felt certain that he would not gain
any more than the 1 VP for ousting you. I don't understand why this
would be so certain that he'd go for the wrong end of a 3-2 split
instead. From the way you tell it, it was because the rest of the
table sided with Brad over the earlier deal and would have cooperated
to screw Paul. Were the other three players friends of Brad's or
what?

I hear that the final of the recent UK tournament was dominated by
recriminations over a deal which went sour - a player played Fame on
another after agreeing to leave him alone for four turns. I have the
impression that unpleasantness of this kind is routine in VTES and it
sounds awful. It's not Succubus Club which is the problem but the
whole deal-making, my-word-is-my-bond culture.

Andrew

I just posted a document to the vtesinla.org site that will hopefully at
least let players know what to expect and how we'll rule such things. I
will, of course, modify this if LSJ has any relevant comments on the
subject. Here's that section from the document:
**********************
Card Layed Is A Card Played--Well, Sort Of

All actions are fully defined upon announcement. If the action cannot be
performed in the manner that it was defined then the card may be returned to
the hand.

Eamples of Fully Defining Actions:

You must announce how much blood you wish to take off a minion via minion
tap before replacing the card. "I Minion Tap Arika for 8".

Carlotta Giovanni must announce with which specific card from your hand will
be exchanged for which specific card from your ash heap.

Examples of Illegally Defined Actions:

If you announce a Govern the Unaligned at Superior and then realize that
your minion has inferior dominate, you are not required to play the card in
the inferior form.

If you accidentally play a Golconda on a minion of 7 capacity and then
realize your error, you are not forced to play the Golconda on some other
minion at the table of 8 capacity or more.

If you drop a deflection to the table and then change your mind *before*
fully announcing the card's effect (who you are deflecting to), you may
return the card to your hand.
*****************

-Robert

In article <9fjrld$uc$1...@taliesin.netcom.net.uk>,

Roger Carhult <rogc...@student.luth.se> wrote:
>I have a question about breaking deals.

[snip]

Accepting, declining to accept, and breaking deals are not covered in
the rules. Each player is therefore free to make, accept, decline or
break deals as he or she chooses.

The only global bar to this is prior explicit collusion.

Trust, or the lack of it, in the other player is part of your judgement.

You use your judgement (based on previous experience) to determine
whether or not to attempt to block the Malkavian who's bleeding you.

You make that decision based on cards in hand, your knowledge of what's
in your deck, the table composition, what cards you've seen your
Malkavian predator play to date, and -- emphasis added -- your
judgement built up from how things have gone in similar situations
from prior games.

It would be ludicrous to claim that decisions based on experience gained
in prior games are 'acting on outside interests;' player experience
is one of the things tested in tournaments.

Similarly:

-an extremely risk-averse player could refuse to accept any
offered deal, regardless of knowledge/trust in the player offering.

-an extremely risk-favorable player could accept any offered deal,
regardless of past betrayals by the person offering.

Given these two extreme (but not inconceivable) possibilities, any
response to a non-collusive deal is perfectly acceptable. The only
things restricted by the tourney rules in re deals are:

Deal terms based on game externals (a round 1 action by person A
exchanged for a future round 2 action by person B, or explicitly
teaming up to deny a player/decktype VPs to the detriment of one
or both deal partner's position in the current game) and

Deals based on prior collusion (A and B agree to act in thus-and-such
a way when they sit at the same table).

While prior knowledge of a person offering you a deal can serve as
a metric of whether to accept a deal or not, and I would prefer,
ceteris paribus, that people who play together not have such
an advantage over people who don't, V:tES is a social game and
we're all going to have to be adults about it. I don't believe the
advantage to be that large.

But I should mention that such a 'home turf advantage' certainly
extends well beyond deal acceptance/refusal. It also conveys:

-What types of deck a person likes to play. This is how I got ousted
first at KublaCon. Ian Lee is a strong player, and all respect to him,
but he has a strong penchant for choosing the interesting deck over
the effective deck, and I (very mistakenly) did not consider him the
strongest threat at the table. This affected how I Restructured the table.

-How many copies of what card a person owns. I would be
very chary of intercepting Noal McDonald's Kindred Spirits action,
for instance, because we all _know_ he's mad for Deranges and I would
want to save intercept/untap for that.

-Play style. This goes beyond deck type. If I know one of my local
players is very risk-averse and distractible, I can tune my play
to irritate that player and possibly goad them into making a mistake.

There seems to be a great deal of confusion between out-of-game
considerations and out-of-game knowledge. I would say that B, knowing
A to be a bad dealer, is free to use that knowledge to decline or break a
deal.
Think about it this way, if B faces A in the second game knowing from
the first game that A has a combat deck, he surely could not be
punished for discarding a deflection at the end of his first turn.
He could, I imagine, be punished for coming across the table to
take his revenge from the previous outing, with votes and bum's
rushes and whatever. But maybe not even then ***.

Perhaps B (having never had his deal broken before)
now gets to exercise his policy of not honoring deals
with people he knows to have broken deals.

> But also if he's allowed to break the deal then he's revenging for out-of
> game purposes and not trying to win (say the deal was more or less
> beneficial to him in that game (naturally since else u don't make deals)).

Presumably you make deals to help you win, and if you break them,
you break them when doing so increases your chance to win.
In that sense, this is not a useful question.

***
Here's my take in general. If I see a guy at my table break a
deal or deal dishonestly, he has my attention, even from
across the table. To some extent this is because I prefer a
stable table environment to work from, and if I know a guy
will lie, I have to always assume he will do the worst to me.
For instance, I have no need to ask a dishonest guy who
he might use Banishment on, I have to assume it will be
on my vampire, even across the table, and asking him is useless.
I have to block if I can, every time. Having to expend
resources in this way over the long term is not my easiest
path to victory, so I'll do what I can to oust that dishonest
guy as soon as I can, even across the table.

This play style may be unworkable in a tournament environment,
I'll probably never know, but it is a legitimate outlook on the game.
And as far as I can conceive, it should not get me into any trouble
with judges enforcing the new tournament rules.

- Jason Bell

The problems come through the way people play the game, rather than the

ambiguous play.

asking players to delineate the exact nature of any controversial
actions. I've done this in a number of games:

etc.

people who are unsure/new

> Card Layed Is A Card Played--Well, Sort Of

> All actions are fully defined upon announcement. If the action cannot be
> performed in the manner that it was defined then the card may be returned to
> the hand.

More broadly: the effects of a card are fully defined (specified, chosen,
named, etc.) when the card is played, as a part of the "play" of a card.

This means, for instance, that the target of a Haven Uncovered or the
'X' of a Secret Horde is declared before players decide whether to play
a Sudden Reversal or not. If the terms were not a part of the play of a
card, then this would not be the case, by card text on Sudden Reversal.

If the play is illegal as defined, then the play is illegal. The player
is under no obligation to redefine the play to be legal, but is merely
subject to whatever penalties are appropriate for a mis-played card
(i.e., the improper showing of a card-in-hand to other players and
possibly the intentional misrepresentation of a card).

> Eamples of Fully Defining Actions:
>
> You must announce how much blood you wish to take off a minion via minion
> tap before replacing the card. "I Minion Tap Arika for 8".

Sure, but that's not an "action". :-)

Also note that if Arika has only 7 blood, then the play is illegal and you
simply take the card back. You are not forced to choose another number
nor are you forceed to choose a different vampire you control with 8 or more
blood.

> Carlotta Giovanni must announce with which specific card from your hand will
> be exchanged for which specific card from your ash heap.
>
> Examples of Illegally Defined Actions:
>
> If you announce a Govern the Unaligned at Superior and then realize that
> your minion has inferior dominate, you are not required to play the card in
> the inferior form.
>
> If you accidentally play a Golconda on a minion of 7 capacity and then
> realize your error, you are not forced to play the Golconda on some other
> minion at the table of 8 capacity or more.
>
> If you drop a deflection to the table and then change your mind *before*
> fully announcing the card's effect (who you are deflecting to), you may
> return the card to your hand.

Correct for all, and you would be subject to the penalty for improperly
displaying a card from your hand in each case.

if you're going to do that, enter a deal that will give you a
significant advantage if you BREAK it, or will suddenly screw him
silly. Take all his minions with the Succubus Club, for example, and
then refuse to trade the SC back to him on your untap. No matter who
eventually ousts him, you -certainly- are in much better shape by
breaking that deal, and you've definitely got your revenge.

Normally, swatting at someone cross-table is frowned upon because you
gain no actual benefit from the situation. In a case such as the
above, where you gain 4 of his minions while he is sure to be ousted,
things are a wee bit different. Same with cross-table Grave Robbing:
you gain a minion, which nobody can argue isn't a substantial benefit
to YOUR game... however much your grandprey absolutely, positively
NEEDED Arika to survive.

>that was made in the same round, but the deal you now break in return was
>very beneficial to you? You could argue that you think it's more important
>for you to punish deal-breakers and that in the long term your position
>should benefit from this more than you lost from breaking the beneficial
>deal although it cannot really be proven...?

just "breaking a deal" is very, very vague, and as such, can't be
answered properly. Such things -must- be dealt with on a case-by-case
basis, for example:

If you make a deal with your grandprey to rescue his vampire in return
for him rescuing yours, and then you don't rescue his, YES, you screw
him up, but you also gain a benefit - you don't waste 2 blood and a
minion action, and you got your own vamp back for free. This is
perfectly within your self-interest.

If you make a deal with someone along the lines of "Since you're going
to be ousted, I'll Dramatic Upheaval behind your predator and oust him
for you, and then I'll let you oust your next two prey as long as you
roll over for me at the end of the game: 3-2 split", then things
become a bit more complicated. If you then call the Dramatic
Upheaval, but don't even make the ATTEMPT to oust (ie. "breaking the
deal"), you've just essentially given your NEW prey a VP and 6 pool.
This is a really, really stupid action causing notable harm to your
own position, and unless you could come up with a VERY good reason,
I'd give you a warning for it.

See the difference? I don't care how much you want to "punish"
deal-breakers... intending to have a "reputation" in the long term is
an out-of-game consideration. You should be playing to win the
current game. Actually, if you want to "punish" him, you should make
the deal, then let him weaken his prey a bit more and break the deal
THEN so you could get all the VPs, or just let him die from your
cross-table position where it doesn't really matter to you. "I COULD
make this deal and save you, but I don't trust you to keep deals, so
you're going to just have to die. Sorry."

Dippy - you just go for the place, hence breaking deals is not required
(but may be useful under some circumstances).

V:TES (under the You Must Get All The Victory Points interpretation of
the rules, which is not supported by LSJ's official position) - you must
get all VPs, hence you must backstab.

Difference == obvious.

Hence, comparisons to Diplomacy in this instance are irrelevant, since
it is a *completely* different set of circumstances. You are *not*
required to backstab, whereas under a VP Maximise interpretation you
would be, thus creating a paradox around most deals. (Must backstab,
therefore can't have made deal.)

It is useful if people consider the implications of there "Look, it
works this way in Random Other Game" before making them. Diplomacy
works in a very different fashion to the proposed interpretation.
